Celebrity Gossip
[1] It’s 2023 and Joe Jonas has filed for divorce from Sophie Turner after four years of
marriage. Other personalities, including Taylor Swift and Joe Alwyn, Ariana Grande
and Dalton Gomez, as well as Hugh Jackman and Deborra Lee all split up. In fact, so
many high-profile pairs have called it quits that some people have deemed 2023 ‘The
Year of Celebrity Breakups.’
[2] Logically speaking, we shouldn’t be interested in this kind of scandalous speculation,
this celebrity gossip. The inner lives of celebrities have next to nothing to do with us,
after all: we’re unlikely ever to meet them, and their romantic relationships have no
bearing on how our own lives unravel, down here in the ‘real’ world. “And yet we are
interested, even if we’re reluctant to admit it,” says Dr. Alice Leppert, a media and
communications professor who focuses on stardom and celebrity culture.
[3] These public figures represent a lot of our highest goals, declares clinical psychologist
and breakup coach Dr. Andrea Liner. They tend to be attractive, wealthy, and
considered successful, which many people assume makes them invulnerable to a lot of
life’s problems. “So, when we find out that beautiful, gorgeous, wealthy celebrities are
getting cheated on or divorcing or breaking up, it kind of humanizes them and can be
validating for us to see that they have problems, too,” she says. “But it can also confuse
us because we think that they shouldn’t be having problems like that if they’ve achieved
these levels of success. Part of the problem is that celebrities may often perform an image
or identity that doesn’t always align with their authentic selves,” she adds. Their marital
problems can come as a shock if all the public saw was a happy family. Liner says that’s
especially true because celebrities share so much of their lives online, creating an “almost
artificial sense of intimacy” that obscures what’s happening behind the scenes.

[4] Gossip is so central to our cultural psyche that the American Psychological
Association (APA) has its own definition. According to the APA, gossip consists of
personal talk or communication about information that’s often not proven to be true,
and it may be (but is not necessarily) scandalous in content or malicious in intention.
Gossip impacts group bonding and has big implications for the transmission and
reinforcement of cultural norms, too.
[5] But why? What purpose does gossip serve? What function is it fulfilling in our
society? Put simply, why do we care?
[6] “There are some people who try to classify gossip as negative or critical discussion
about other people, but really, gossip is just sharing social information with each other,”
says author and professor of psychology Dr. David Ludden. “Anytime you’re talking
about people who aren’t present, it’s gossip,” he says. “We’re social animals and we need
to be able to know what’s going on in social environments, so gossip is very helpful,”
says Ludden, who studies the psychology of language and how it shapes and is shaped by
our social world. Basically, gossip can help you go into social encounters more prepared
for what’s coming. “I don’t have to have an encounter with someone directly to have
some idea what they’re like, because other people are telling me about their encounters
with them,” says Ludden.
[7] It can also be a way to build relationships: “Sharing gossip can bond people socially,”
says Dr. Stephen Benning from the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. Benning published
a study in 2019 which found that gossip provides a currency of private information that
creates a shared sense of the community holding that information. So, gossip is
particularly compelling for people who are seeking to connect with others.

[8] But it’s not all so innocent. Benning found that we’re also attracted to gossip for
some other reasons: attacking people’s social standing and their position in social
networks (what is called ‘negative influence’), merely elevating our own social status, or
simply trying to be included in a social network that we previously weren’t. Similarly,
Ludden says that “lots of the bad gossip is done in an attempt to make ourselves feel
better than the person we’re talking about. That’s not a healthy approach to building a
sense of self-esteem.”
[9] Negative influence (talking badly about someone or trying to cut them down) was a
clear motive for some people on certain occasions. Yet, the study found that this was
actually the weakest motivation that led people to gossip. Gathering and validating
information about the person being gossiped about was the strongest.
[10] There’s also some evidence suggesting that negative gossip can have a positive
impact on social groups and promote cooperation (though perhaps not in the most
altruistic way). In an article published in the journal Psychological Science, researchers
found that when people communicated reputational information about others (the
researchers’ definition of “gossiped”), others tended to interact with people who were
portrayed as cooperative and ostracize those who were portrayed as selfish. As a result,
those who were ostracized tended to change their behavior and act more cooperatively.
[11] What motivates us to gossip about A-listers we don’t socialize with?
[12] Ludden says that just because we’ve never met these celebrities doesn’t mean we
don’t have relationships with them: “What we do is we create parasocial relationships —
imaginary relationships with a singer or athlete whose successes we’ve followed and
celebrated.” Like gossip itself, these parasocial relationships can be healthy or unhealthy
depending on the circumstances. They can fill the gaps in our real-world relationships,
and they’re a risk-free way to feel connected to others, since you can’t be rejected by
someone who’s not actually in a relationship with you.

[13] Gossiping about these celebrities can be a similarly low-stakes way to feel
connected, since the information you’re sharing doesn’t pose a risk to you or a member
of your social circle. “It can feel uncomfortable and vulnerable to share information
about your own worlds,” Benning says. “Gossiping about celebrities is a safer way to
interact with a date, to ingratiate yourself to a group at parties, or to feel part of a new
team at work.” It can also serve as a form of stress relief. “When life is overwhelming,
focusing on celebrity gossip can be a way to numb out our feelings of dissatisfaction,
unhappiness, or stress,” says Benning. “Scrolling through celebrity gossip puts us in a
dissociated state where we can take breaks from difficult feelings.”
[14] But just like regular gossip, sometimes the motivation behind celebrity gossip is to
make ourselves feel better than others. “Celebrity gossip is a safe way to snack on
schadenfreude (the delight in the misfortune of others),” says Benning. “It feels a lot less
shameful to admit we enjoy watching celebrity misfortunes than to admit we enjoy
watching the misfortunes of family and friends.”

Paragraph 4（第四段）
Topic Sentence（主題句）
Gossip is so central to our cultural psyche that the American Psychological
Association (APA) has its own definition.
八卦在我們的文化心理中如此核心，以致美國心理學會（APA）也對它有自己
的定義。
Definition（定義）
According to the APA, gossip consists of personal talk or communication about
information that’s often not proven to be true, and it may be (but is not
necessarily) scandalous in content or malicious in intention.
根據 APA 的定義，八卦是指關於個人資訊的談話或交流，而這些資訊往往未
被證實為真；其內容可能具有醜聞性質，或其意圖可能帶有惡意，但並非必然
如此。

Gossip impacts group bonding and has big implications for the transmission
and reinforcement of cultural norms, too.
八卦也會影響群體凝聚，並且對文化規範的傳播與強化具有重大影響。

Additional Evidence（補充證據）
There’s also some evidence suggesting that negative gossip can have a positive
impact on social groups and promote cooperation (though perhaps not in the

In an article published in the journal Psychological Science, researchers found
that when people communicated reputational information about others (the
researchers’ definition of “gossiped”), others tended to interact with people who
were portrayed as cooperative and ostracize those who were portrayed as selfish.

與被描述為合作的人互動，並排斥那些被描述為自私的人。

As a result, those who were ostracized tended to change their behavior and act
more cooperatively.

Paragraph 12（第十二段）
Expert View（專家觀點）
Ludden says that just because we’ve never met these celebrities doesn’t mean we
don’t have relationships with them:
Ludden 說，即使我們從未見過這些名人，也不代表我們和他們沒有關係：
Explanation（解釋）
“What we do is we create parasocial relationships — imaginary relationships
with a singer or athlete whose successes we’ve followed and celebrated.”
「我們所做的是創造擬社會關係——也就是和某位歌手或運動員建立想像中
的關係，而我們一直追隨並慶祝他們的成功。」
Elaboration（闡述）
Like gossip itself, these parasocial relationships can be healthy or unhealthy
depending on the circumstances.
就像八卦本身一樣，這些擬社會關係可以是健康的，也可以是不健康的，視
乎具體情況而定。
Explanation（解釋）
They can fill the gaps in our real-world relationships, and they’re a risk-free way
to feel connected to others, since you can’t be rejected by someone who’s not
actually in a relationship with you.
它們可以填補我們現實人際關係中的空缺，也是一種沒有風險的連結方式，
因為一個實際上並沒有和你建立關係的人，是不可能拒絕你的。

misfortune of others),” says Benning.

第一層：文章用 2023 年大量 celebrity breakups 開場。
第一段列出 Joe Jonas / Sophie Turner、Taylor Swift / Joe Alwyn、Ariana Grande /
Dalton Gomez、Hugh Jackman / Deborra Lee 等名人分手或離婚事件，
建立背景：2023 年被一些人稱為 “The Year of Celebrity Breakups”。
這把讀者帶入一個現象：
名人私生活明明和我們沒有直接關係，但大家仍然關注。
第二層：文章提出矛盾。
第二段說，理性上我們不該對明星私生活感興趣，
因為我們大多不會認識他們，
他們的感情和我們自己的生活也沒有直接影響。
可是 Alice Leppert 指出，大家的確感興趣，只是有時不願承認。
這就形成全文要解釋的核心問題：why do we care?
第三層：明星的完美形象使他們的失敗更有心理衝擊。
第三段用 Andrea Liner 的說法解釋：明星代表很多人心中的最高目標，
例如美貌、財富、成功。大家容易以為這些條件使他們免受普通人的痛苦。
當他們也被背叛、離婚、分手時，一方面會 humanize them，
另一方面也會 confuse us。
原因是明星常在社交媒體上表演一種幸福、成功、完美的形象，
讓公眾看不到幕後真相。

第四層：文章把 gossip 重新定義。
第四至第十段從心理學和社會功能角度分析 gossip。
APA 把 gossip 定義為關於他人的個人談話，資訊常常未經證實，
也可能帶有醜聞性或惡意。
Ludden 進一步把 gossip 定義得更廣：只要談論不在場的人，就是 gossip。
這使 gossip 從「壞話」變成一種社會資訊交換。
第五層：gossip 有好處，也有陰暗面。
第六、七段說 gossip 可以讓人更了解社交環境，也可以促進社交連結。
第八、九段轉向陰暗面：
有些 gossip 是為了攻擊他人社會地位、提升自己地位、加入某個社交網絡。
不過第九段也指出，最強的動機其實是 gathering and validating information，
而攻擊他人反倒是最弱動機。
第十段再補充，負面 gossip 有時也能促進合作，
因為群體會避開自私者，迫使他們改變行為。
第六層：celebrity gossip 的特殊吸引力。
第十一至十四段回到明星八卦。
Ludden 說人們會和明星形成 parasocial relationships，即想像中的關係。Benning
說談明星八卦風險低，
因為這些資訊不牽涉自己身邊的人，可以用來和朋友、約會對象、同事建立
連結，也可以作為壓力緩解。
最後，Benning 補充 celebrity gossip 也能讓人安全地享受 schadenfreude，即看到
他人不幸而感到某種快感。

原文定位
Paragraph 3：
“Part of the problem is that celebrities may often perform an image or identity that
doesn’t always align with their authentic selves... Their marital problems can come as a
shock if all the public saw was a happy family. Liner says that’s especially true because
celebrities share so much of their lives online, creating an ‘almost artificial sense of
intimacy’ that obscures what’s happening behind the scenes.”
題目問甚麼
題目問的是 “why”，
而且特別引用 “come as a shock”。所以答案要解釋 shock 的原因。
原文的邏輯分成三層：
1. Celebrities perform an image or identity.
2. The image may not match their authentic selves.
3. The public may only see a happy family online.
4. This creates artificial intimacy and hides behind-the-scenes problems.
5. When hidden marital problems appear, the public feels shocked.

答案如何成立
1. 如果公眾一直看到某明星家庭幸福、伴侶恩愛、親子和諧，
2. 公眾便容易建立一種印象：這家人很幸福。
3. 可是 paragraph 3 說 celebrity image can be performed，
4. 意思是這種形象有表演、包裝、選擇性展示的成分。
5. 再加上社交媒體會加強這種錯覺。
6. 明星分享很多日常片段，讓粉絲覺得自己好像了解他們、親近他們
7. Liner 稱這為 “almost artificial sense of intimacy”。
所以當婚姻問題、離婚、出軌等消息出現時，公眾的反應是：
我以為他們很幸福
我以為我了解他們
結果幕後情況完全不同
這就是 shock 的來源。

(ii) Some gossip may be harmful or upset people.
【有些 gossip 可能有害或令人不快。】
答案：T
先看這句 statement 聲稱了甚麼
這句 statement 其實有三個很重要的邏輯部分：
第一，Some gossip
它沒有說 all gossip。 它只說「有些 gossip」。
第二，may be
它沒有說 gossip 一定會傷害人。 它只說「可能」有害或令人不快。
第三，harmful or upset people

為甚麼 足以支持
“malicious in intention”
“harmful or upset people”?
Malicious 的核心意思是帶有惡意、懷著不良意圖、想令別人受損或受傷。
Intention 指意圖、目的、動機。
所以 malicious in intention 不是中性描述。
它不是單純「分享資訊」。
它指某些 gossip 的說話目的可能帶有攻擊性或傷害性。
如果某一段 personal talk about someone 是 malicious in intention，這已經代表：
說話者可能想貶低那個人。
說話者可能想破壞那個人的名聲。
說話者可能想令那個人被排斥。
說話者可能想令其他人用負面眼光看那個人。
說話者可能想把某些私人資訊用來傷害人。
那麼，這種 gossip 當然 may be harmful。
也當然 may upset people。
注意這裡仍然是 may。
我們不是推論「每一次 malicious gossip 都一定成功傷害人」。
我們只是說，既然原文承認 gossip 有時可能帶有惡意，
statement 說「有些 gossip 可能有害或令人不快」就有文本支持。

為甚麼 “But” 是答案核心
“But” 是英文中最直接的 contrast marker。
它告訴讀者：接下來的內容會和前面的正面描述形成對比。
前面：gossip can bond people socially
後面：gossip can also be used to attack status or elevate oneself
所以 “But” 承擔了段落功能轉向。
“not all so innocent” 的作用
“not all so innocent” 不是單一連接詞，但它也顯示 contrast。它暗示：
前面看起來 innocent / positive
接下來會指出 less innocent / darker motives
所以若題目要求 words，答案可寫：
“But” / “not all so innocent”

最後總結
第1–3題訓練局部細節與同義短語辨認。
Joe Jonas filed for divorce，2023 被稱為 breakup year，是因為 many high-profile
pairs split up / called it quits。
第4–5題訓練指代與語境理解。
“real world” 指 ordinary people’s lives；it 要回看前面整個概念，不可只捉最近名
詞。
第6–7題訓練原因鏈與流程圖精準填字。
明星的 happy public image、online sharing、artificial intimacy 使 public 看不到
behind the scenes。流程圖答案要同時符合原文與語法。
第8題訓練 T/F/NG 判斷。
Often 不等於 all；may scandalous / malicious 支持 some harmful；cultural norms 不
等於 different cultures；group bonding 反駁 no role in relationships。
第9–14題訓練 discourse marker、社會功能、metaphor、main reason、
vocabulary in context。
Put simply = simplify; gossip prepares us by social information; But marks contrast; cut
them down is metaphor; strongest motivation = gathering information; act / promote /
result / portrayed 要看詞性。
第15–18題訓練 celebrity-specific vocabulary and concept。
A-listers = top celebrities; parasocial relationships = imaginary connection; benefit = fill
gaps + risk-free connection; difficult feelings = stress / dissatisfaction / unhappiness。
第19–21題訓練全篇意圖、專家立場、段落配對。
作者目的不是批評 gossip，而是解釋 motives。四位專家中，Leppert 只指出人
們有興趣，未談 benefit；Liner、Ludden、Benning 都指出可能好處。段落配對要
看 idea-level paraphrase，不可只靠明星名字或單字重複。
